paragraphs: This paper asks why surrounding visual elements can change both the perceived orientation of a target and confidence in that judgment. These are related but distinct effects: a target can appear tilted incorrectly, and its orientation can become harder to judge reliably. The authors seek a common computational explanation for both.

Their Bayesian model combines evidence from the image with a prior favoring smoothness. This prior expresses an expectation about how orientations fit together across space. The model explicitly considers the positions of the stimuli, allowing their arrangement to influence orientation estimates rather than treating surrounding orientations as an unordered collection.

The authors report that this framework explains a range of tilt findings, including results in which image properties systematically affect both bias and confidence. Its contribution is to connect perceptual distortions and uncertainty within one inference account. The findings support smoothness-based Bayesian estimation as an explanation for these observations, without establishing it as the only possible perceptual mechanism.
neurips-2005-a-bayesian-framework-for-ti.tldr: A Bayesian model with a smoothness prior explains how visual context can alter both perceived tilt and confidence.

paragraphs: Female crickets locate potential mates by moving toward the songs produced by males, a behavior called phonotaxis. The paper studies the auditory processing behind this ability by building an electronic model. Its aim is to reproduce aspects of the biological process in physical circuitry and compare that implementation with existing understanding of cricket hearing.

The implementation uses analogue very large scale integration, or aVLSI: an integrated circuit that models the process through analogue electronics. This gives the researchers a hardware realization to test alongside simulation. The central question is whether the circuit's responses agree with both the simulated model and observations of the animal's behavior and physiology.

The authors report agreement across those comparisons, supporting the circuit as a model of the auditory process studied. They also describe an ongoing extension toward use on a robot together with previously modeled neural circuitry. That extension is intended to help investigate the complete pathway from sensing sound to movement; the abstract presents it as work in progress.
neurips-2005-an-avlsi-cricket-ear-model-.tldr: An analogue integrated circuit reproduces aspects of cricket hearing, with tests agreeing with simulation and known biology.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms update as examples arrive and are often fast, economical with memory, and straightforward to implement. Many tasks, however, are naturally approached using an available collection of training examples. This paper studies how to convert an online learner into a batch learner while retaining the appeal of the underlying online algorithm.

The authors first organize three existing conversion techniques within a unified account. Those techniques do not use the training data during the conversion itself. Building on them, the paper introduces conversions that explicitly use data-dependent generalization bounds. These bounds guide the choice of a predictor by estimating how well it should perform beyond the training examples.

The resulting procedure searches for hypotheses with low risk by minimizing those bounds. The authors provide an analysis and report experiments in which their data-driven conversions consistently outperform the data-independent alternatives. This supports using information in the observed data to guide conversion, with the reported consistency describing the experimental comparisons rather than a universal performance guarantee.
neurips-2005-data-driven-online-to-batch.tldr: Using data-dependent generalization bounds improves online-to-batch conversion in the paper's experiments.

paragraphs: Neural activity can evolve in ways that are not directly explained by external stimulation. Such dynamics may reflect recurrent circuitry and could reveal how the brain carries out internally driven operations. This paper examines premotor cortex activity during the delay between learning a movement target and receiving the cue to begin moving, a period believed to involve motor planning.

The authors represent the underlying activity with a low-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system. Its recurrent structure describes how an internal state evolves, while a stochastic point-process output connects that state to observed spikes. This separates the proposed underlying dynamics from the individual firing events used to infer them.

The paper presents and validates latent-variable methods that jointly estimate model parameters and a separate dynamical trajectory for each trial. The methods are applied to recordings from a chronically implanted 96-electrode array in monkeys performing delayed reaches. The reported ability to capture these dynamics supports studying coordinated neural activity through a compact evolving state, while preserving differences between trials.
neurips-2005-extracting-dynamical-struct.tldr: A latent dynamical model captures trial-specific structure in premotor neural activity during delayed reaching.

paragraphs: The paper presents RunBot, a planar two-legged robot controlled entirely through a biologically inspired reflex system. The goal is to combine neural control mechanisms with the body's mechanics to achieve fast walking and learn controller settings while moving. Its sensor and motor neuron models provide local reflexes without a controller that tracks prescribed positions or trajectories.

This design lets the robot use its natural dynamics during important parts of each step. The authors also apply policy-gradient reinforcement learning to adjust the reflex controller's parameters in real time. Learning therefore changes the settings of a working walking controller while the robot continues to interact with its own mechanics.

After a few minutes of online learning, RunBot reaches 3.5 leg-lengths per second. The authors report this as faster in relative terms than other biped robots and comparable to the fastest human walking. They also report a broad region of stable walking conditions. These results support their combined reflex-and-biomechanics strategy, while their claim of a first purely reflexive dynamic walker is explicitly qualified by their knowledge.
neurips-2005-fast-biped-walking-with-a-r.tldr: RunBot combines reflex control, natural body dynamics, and online policy learning to achieve fast, stable biped walking.

paragraphs: This paper investigates when choosing where to collect data can improve regression. An active learner selects queries or sample locations using the results of earlier queries. That flexibility can make its observations more useful for estimating a function, but the paper's central question is which settings permit a substantial advantage over passive learning.

The authors analyze fundamental performance limits for active and passive learning in two nonparametric function classes. This comparison identifies regimes where active learning can achieve faster decreases in error as data accumulate. The result is conditional: the benefit depends on the regime being studied, rather than following automatically from the ability to choose samples.

Beyond characterizing what is theoretically possible, the paper gives a practical algorithm that exploits adaptive sampling and provably improves on classical passive techniques in the relevant setting. The authors identify field estimation with wireless sensor networks and fault-line detection as promising applications. These are presented as areas of potential use, while the established contribution is the statistical analysis and the algorithm's proved improvement.
neurips-2005-faster-rates-in-regression-.tldr: The paper identifies regression regimes where adaptive sampling yields provably faster error reduction than passive learning.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes prediction error on genuinely unseen cases from standard generalization error. Standard generalization evaluates performance under the overall data distribution, whereas off-training-set error focuses on cases absent from the training set. The authors show that this latter error can differ substantially from training error with high probability, even when the sample is large.

They derive a data-dependent bound connecting off-training-set error to standard generalization error. The argument uses a new bound on the missing mass: the probability assigned to cases that the training sample has not included. For small samples, their missing-mass bound is stronger than existing bounds based on Good–Turing estimators.

Experiments on UCI datasets show that the bound provides nontrivial generalization guarantees in many practical cases. This makes the distinction between new observations and previously unseen cases something that can be assessed using data. The authors also use the results to challenge certain pessimistic claims in the No Free Lunch literature, rather than rejecting every claim associated with that literature.
neurips-2005-generalization-to-unseen-ca.tldr: A new missing-mass bound helps quantify classification error specifically on cases absent from the training set.

paragraphs: An incremental learning algorithm produces a sequence of candidate predictors as it works through training data. This paper studies the risk of hypotheses selected from that resulting collection. The question concerns the predictive quality of a selected hypothesis, making the sequence generated during learning the central object of the analysis.

The contribution is a theoretical risk bound, described by the authors as the strongest known for this selection setting. As the title indicates, the focus is on risk tail bounds: guarantees concerning the possibility of larger prediction risk. The result therefore addresses how much assurance can be attached to a predictor selected from the online learning process.

The authors emphasize that their proof uses techniques substantially different from standard analyses based on uniform convergence. Uniform convergence arguments seek control across a collection of candidate hypotheses; this paper establishes its stated bound through another proof approach. Its significance lies in strengthening the guarantee available for selected online hypotheses and broadening the analytical methods used to obtain such guarantees.
neurips-2005-improved-risk-tail-bounds-f.tldr: The paper proves a stronger risk guarantee for hypotheses selected from an incremental learner's outputs using a different proof approach.

paragraphs: Word frequencies in natural language follow a strikingly uneven pattern: some words occur often, while many others occur rarely. The paper argues that standard statistical language models fail to capture this power-law behavior. It proposes a framework that changes how a generative model produces repeated word occurrences while retaining the underlying generative model.

The key addition is an adaptor that produces the desired pattern of token frequencies. Tokens are individual occurrences, whereas types are distinct forms. The authors show that using a particular stochastic process, the Pitman–Yor process, as the adaptor provides a justification for the appearance of type frequencies in formal language analysis.

This connects a modeling choice about repetition to the question of how distinct forms should influence statistical learning. The authors also report improved performance for an unsupervised morphology model, which learns aspects of word structure without labeled examples. The contribution thus combines a framework for producing power-law frequencies, an explanation of type-based quantities, and an empirical improvement in the stated language-learning task.
neurips-2005-interpolating-between-types.tldr: A Pitman–Yor adaptor models power-law word frequencies, explains the role of type counts, and improves unsupervised morphology learning.

paragraphs: This paper approaches clustering by asking how informative unknown cluster labels can be about the observed training patterns. It uses soft clustering, so the model describes cluster assignments probabilistically. The objective is to maximize mutual information between patterns and labels by adjusting the parameters of a constrained probability model for assigning labels.

The constraints give the information objective a spatial structure. Patterns near particular unknown vectors in feature space are encouraged to receive similar cluster assignments. Learning therefore involves finding an informative labeling while respecting the specified relationship between feature-space proximity and cluster membership. The vectors themselves are not supplied as known cluster representatives.

The authors also explain how the approach can learn an affinity matrix through the parameters of a kernelized encoder. This means that the relationships used for clustering can be learned within the same formulation. The procedure avoids computing eigenvalues of Gram matrices, which the authors identify as a potential advantage for large datasets. They present that scalability benefit as a possibility, rather than a demonstrated universal speed advantage.
neurips-2005-kernelized-infomax-clusteri.tldr: An information-maximizing soft clustering method learns kernel affinities without computing Gram-matrix eigenvalues.

paragraphs: Detailed neuron models can explain how a cell transforms inputs into outputs, but many parameters usually require manual adjustment. This paper proposes automatic estimation of several important quantities: channel densities across the membrane, synaptic input over space and time, reversal potentials, conductances between compartments, and noise levels. The aim is to make these complex models easier to fit and interpret.

The method assumes access to voltage measurements across time and a contiguous dendritic region, an approximate kinetic description of its channels and synapses, and the region's morphology. Given those inputs, the first four parameter groups can be inferred together using constrained linear regression. Standard algorithms solve that regression efficiently without local-minimum problems despite the complexity of the underlying neuronal dynamics.

Noise levels can be estimated separately using standard techniques. The authors demonstrate accuracy on several model datasets and describe how to quantify uncertainty in the estimates. The contribution is therefore a tractable estimation formulation under explicit measurement and modeling assumptions, with demonstrated accuracy on modeled data rather than a stated validation on experimental neuron recordings.
neurips-2005-large-scale-biophysical-par.tldr: Given voltage data, morphology, and approximate kinetics, constrained linear regression can jointly estimate many biophysical neuron parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when several sources provide limited amounts of data and each source may have a different corruption rate. The central decision is which sources to use. A source contributes observations, but their quality also matters, so the learning problem includes choosing the data as well as estimating the desired quantity.

The authors analyze two basic tasks. The first is estimating a coin's bias, meaning its probability of producing one of its two outcomes. The second is learning a classifier when some training labels are corrupted. These settings let the paper examine source selection for both probability estimation and prediction from noisy labels.

For each task, the authors develop what they describe as a complete theory of which data sources should be included. They also provide efficient algorithms for computing the optimal subset of data. The contribution is therefore both a characterization of the selection problem and a way to carry out that selection, with optimality established for the two studied problems rather than for arbitrary learning tasks.
neurips-2005-learning-from-data-of-varia.tldr: The paper gives theory and efficient algorithms for selecting data sources with different corruption rates in two learning problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a ranking from ordering constraints between groups of training examples. These groups act as classes, and the constraints can specify a partial ordering rather than requiring every class to be ordered against every other. The goal is a ranking function that respects the comparisons supplied by this structure.

The proposed algorithms can maximize a generalized Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney statistic that accounts for the class ordering. This connects the method to familiar ranking objectives: maximizing area under the ROC curve in binary classification is one special case, and an extension for ordinal regression is another. The same formulation therefore covers several related ways to judge ordering quality.

On public benchmarks, the authors report accuracy at least comparable to the then-current state of the art, alongside computation that is several orders of magnitude faster. They also report handling datasets with more than 20,000 examples. These experimental findings support the method's practical appeal for larger ranking problems, while the relative accuracy and speed claims refer to the comparisons performed.
neurips-2005-learning-rankings-via-conve.tldr: Efficient ranking algorithms handle partially ordered classes and show competitive accuracy with major speed gains on public benchmarks.

paragraphs: An octopus arm offers many ways to move and change shape, creating a difficult control problem. The paper explores whether online reinforcement learning can address that complexity. Its subject is a computer simulation of a two-dimensional arm model, which retains a high-dimensional state space despite simplifying the biological limb.

The learning algorithm builds on Gaussian process temporal difference learning, or GPTD. This is a Bayesian approach to policy evaluation: assessing a control policy as part of the learning process. The authors use that approach within an online reinforcement learning algorithm applied to the simulated arm, bringing Bayesian evaluation into a demanding control setting.

They demonstrate the algorithm on several learning tasks with different levels of difficulty. The result establishes its operation in this simulated domain and shows how the approach can be applied to a highly flexible limb model. It does not resolve how a real octopus controls its arms; that biological question motivates the work, while the reported demonstrations concern the simplified computational model.
neurips-2005-learning-to-control-an-octo.tldr: A GPTD-based reinforcement learner tackles several control tasks in a high-dimensional, two-dimensional octopus-arm simulation.

paragraphs: Understanding a population of neurons requires modeling how their firing varies together, not just describing each neuron separately. The paper tackles the difficulty of representing these joint patterns in high-dimensional data. It proposes an energy-based probability model designed to capture correlated population activity without relying on a fully nonparametric description of the entire joint distribution.

The model constructs joint probabilities using learned functions of one-dimensional marginal histograms. Its training procedure combines contrastive divergence with optimization to find suitable directions for those marginals. This gives the model a way to build a richer joint representation from lower-dimensional descriptions chosen during learning.

The authors evaluate the method on motor-cortex recordings, modeling population spike times jointly with two-dimensional hand position. Held-out data receive significantly higher likelihood under their model than under the other models compared. They interpret this as evidence that the model captures firing correlations. The work is presented as a step toward measuring the role of correlations in neural coding and improving decoding, rather than as a demonstrated decoding improvement itself.
neurips-2005-modeling-neural-population-.tldr: An energy-based model achieves higher test-data likelihood for joint neural firing and hand-position data, suggesting it captures population correlations.

paragraphs: Object detectors must learn what an object looks like, but training can also require knowing exactly where each example appears. This paper develops a detector that does not need precise object locations in its training images. It combines the Viola–Jones cascade architecture with a new boosting method called MILBoost.

MILBoost brings cost functions from multiple-instance learning into the AnyBoost framework. This formulation allows object location and scale to be learned together with classifier parameters, rather than requiring exact locations in advance. The authors also adapt its feature-selection criterion to optimize performance within the cascade architecture, connecting the training objective to the detector's structure.

The experiments report a detection rate up to 1.6 times better with MILBoost. That figure describes the largest reported improvement, not a uniform gain across every setting. The authors interpret the improvement as evidence for learning object placement and appearance jointly. The approach thus addresses training annotation requirements and detection performance through the same learning formulation.
neurips-2005-multiple-instance-boosting-.tldr: MILBoost jointly learns object locations, scales, and classifier parameters, with reported detection-rate improvements of up to 1.6 times.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a feature-selection method for regression, where the goal is to predict a numerical target. It uses a feature-weighted version of k-nearest-neighbor prediction. Weighting the inputs changes which examples count as neighbors, allowing the method to identify a useful subset of features while capturing nonlinear relationships between inputs and the target.

The algorithm uses leave-one-out prediction error as a natural form of regularization. In this assessment, each example is predicted without using that example itself as training evidence. The authors explain the method's behavior on synthetic problems, connecting its feature choices to its ability to represent complex dependencies.

They then apply it to predicting hand velocity from spikes recorded in a behaving monkey's motor cortex. Feature selection improves prediction quality in that application. This result supports the method as a practical regression tool and suggests a way to explore neural data through the inputs useful for prediction. The stated finding concerns predictive improvement, rather than a causal explanation of how particular neurons control movement.
neurips-2005-nearest-neighbor-based-feat.tldr: Feature-weighted nearest-neighbor regression selects useful inputs and improves hand-velocity prediction from motor-cortex spikes.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how neuronal populations respond to instantaneous inputs and inputs that change over time. It includes synaptic depression in its mathematical description, making synaptic behavior part of the response calculation. The aim is to understand both population firing and the contribution of synapses to processing incoming information.

The authors derive an evolution equation for the distribution of membrane potentials and obtain formulas for calculating instantaneous firing rates analytically. This population-level description supports an analysis of how input conditions affect the response. Their findings assign background inputs an important role: they can switch processing between accumulating signals over time and detecting signals that arrive together.

The analysis also describes synapses as filters operating across space and time. Both the locations of synapses and the spatial and temporal relationships among inputs matter in this account. In addition, instantaneous input frequency affects response amplitude and phase delay. Together, these conclusions show how the modeled population response depends on background activity, input timing, and spatial organization.
neurips-2005-response-analysis-of-neuron.tldr: An analytical population model with synaptic depression links background activity and input organization to different modes of neural response.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to improve character models for a handwritten script without requiring supplied transcriptions. It also aims to use very little training data specific to the document. The practical objective is better word retrieval: finding occurrences of words within the handwriting using a character model adapted to that document.

The method begins with searches for dictionary words. Those searches identify portions of the document whose transcriptions can be determined unambiguously. The system then extracts templates from those regions and uses them to retrain its character prediction model. Search therefore supplies document-specific training evidence that can improve subsequent search.

The authors report a drastic improvement in word-search retrieval after this retraining. The central contribution is the connection between searching and adaptation: confidently identified text regions become material for improving the model that interprets the handwriting. Although supplied transcriptions are unnecessary, the method still uses a dictionary and the unambiguous regions found through it. The stated outcome concerns retrieval performance for words in the document.
neurips-2005-searching-for-character-mod.tldr: Dictionary searches identify reliable handwriting examples that retrain character models and substantially improve word retrieval.

paragraphs: Sequence and tree kernels let learning algorithms work with the discrete structures found in language. The paper addresses a practical difficulty with these methods: experiments had shown the best results when kernels were restricted to small substructures. Simply including larger structures did not automatically make their extra information useful.

The authors propose statistical feature selection based on mining substructures. Its purpose is to make larger substructures usable by selecting features rather than indiscriminately including them. To keep the procedure efficient, the mining algorithms can be incorporated into the original kernel calculation. Feature selection is therefore connected directly to how structural similarities are computed.

Experiments on real natural-language-processing tasks confirm the problem with conventional kernels and compare the proposed method against a conventional approach. The abstract presents the selection method as enabling effective use of larger substructures, without specifying numerical gains. The contribution is a way to control which structural features enter the kernel while integrating that control into its computation.
neurips-2005-sequence-and-tree-kernels-w.tldr: Statistical substructure mining adds feature selection to sequence and tree kernels so larger language structures can be used effectively.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how different postsynaptic signals could change the learning behavior of local groups of synapses over time. It focuses on dendritic spikes and spikes that propagate back from the cell body. The authors use both signals in a differential Hebbian learning rule that emulates spike-timing-dependent plasticity.

The studied process begins with weak synapses that produce only local dendritic spikes. At this stage, synaptic growth is slow and relatively unspecific. Once the cell body starts firing, stronger and sharper back-propagating spikes dominate the learning rule. The same modeled system then undergoes faster synaptic changes because the postsynaptic signal driving learning has changed.

This transition produces a two-stage winner-take-all mechanism that strengthens the best-correlated inputs. The result suggests that synaptic learning characteristics need not remain fixed: they can shift with the activity generated as learning proceeds. The authors propose that such changing plasticity could substantially expand the computational properties of dendrites or whole neurons, presenting this as an implication of the modeled mechanism.
neurips-2005-temporally-changing-synapti.tldr: A model shows how a shift from dendritic to back-propagating spikes can turn slow synaptic growth into selective competition.

paragraphs: This paper asks how visual search balances conspicuous image features against knowledge of the target. It tests different mixtures of bottom-up and top-down information in a saliency-based model. The model includes an artificial retina and a neuronal population code, allowing the comparison to account for specified biological constraints.

The bottom-up component responds to feature contrast, while the top-down component measures how well features match a stored representation of the target. The authors vary their contributions and compare the model's search behavior with eye movements from human observers performing the same task. This directly connects the weighting question to observed search behavior.

Within this biologically constrained model, purely top-down guidance matches human behavior much more closely than any tested mixture that includes bottom-up information. A mixed model begins to approximate human behavior only after biological constraints, such as the retina, are removed. The finding makes those constraints central to interpreting the comparison; it supports top-down guidance in this task and modeling framework rather than a universal claim about all visual attention.
neurips-2005-the-role-of-top-down-and-bo.tldr: In the tested biologically constrained search model, purely target-driven guidance matches human eye movements better than mixtures including feature contrast.

paragraphs: People often perform a visual discrimination task more easily when relevant features repeat from recent trials. This paper explains that facilitation as adaptation to the statistical structure of the environment. It places the effect within an account of attention in which different visual features contribute to a saliency map that guides selection.

The authors propose a probabilistic model of the environment that is updated after every trial. Their key assumption is that attentional control makes performance more efficient for environmental states that are more likely. Recent experience therefore influences attention by changing what the model expects to encounter, rather than serving only as a record of earlier stimuli.

Under this assumption, the model provides compact explanations for results from four experiments. It also explains why the influence of past experience fades quickly. The contribution is a rational account linking short-lived attentional adjustments to environmental expectations. Its explanatory force depends on the stated relationship between probability and efficient performance, rather than establishing that every attentional effect follows from this principle.
neurips-2005-top-down-control-of-visual-.tldr: A trial-updated probabilistic model explains repetition benefits and their short duration as adaptive control of visual attention.

paragraphs: Kernel methods make it possible to define rich, high-dimensional representations, but those representations raise a selection problem: which parts are relevant to the learning task? This paper considers settings with two views of the same phenomenon. Such views provide a basis for seeking useful relationships between representations before or during classification.

The starting point is a two-stage approach in which kernel canonical correlation analysis, or KCCA, preprocesses the views before a support vector machine performs classification. KCCA had been shown to help classification in this setting. The authors propose SVM-2K, which combines the two stages into a single optimization problem.

The paper presents both theoretical analysis and experiments, reporting encouraging results and insights. Its main contribution is the joint formulation: representation relationships and classification are addressed within one learning problem. The abstract supports this as a promising integration of the existing stages, without claiming that it always outperforms separate preprocessing or that all pairs of views will be equally useful.
neurips-2005-two-view-learning-svm-2k-th.tldr: SVM-2K combines two-view kernel correlation analysis and support vector classification in one optimization.

paragraphs: Even during fixation, small eye and body movements keep the retinal image from remaining perfectly still. Although prolonged retinal stabilization is known to make stimuli fade, this paper asks whether ordinary fixation movements serve a visual purpose over much shorter viewing periods. It examines their effects on retinal input statistics and modeled early visual activity.

With natural images, fixation instability introduces input fluctuations that lack spatial correlations. In a model of the lateral geniculate nucleus, these fluctuations strongly affect neural responses and reduce correlations between cells. This happens even when the simulated cells' contrast sensitivity is not perfectly matched to counteract the power-law spectrum of natural images.

Reduced response correlation has been proposed as a way to discard statistical redundancy in visual input. On that basis, the authors suggest that fixation instability might help establish efficient representations of natural scenes. The modeled decorrelation is the reported result; improved coding efficiency is its proposed interpretation. This makes small gaze movements a possible contributor to visual encoding during natural fixation.
neurips-2005-visual-encoding-with-jitter.tldr: Small fixation movements decorrelate responses in an early-vision model and may help reduce redundancy in natural-image encoding.
